last-7-days.title: The last 7 days before a Semester 3 exam
last-7-days.description: A day-by-day plan for the final week: map the repeated questions, drill numericals, write two full past papers under exam conditions and fix your mistakes.
last-7-days.body:
A week before a Semester 3 exam you cannot relearn a subject, and you do not need to. Across the 22 papers on CampusLoop, the same 15–20 questions per subject come back again and again: RTL and the common bus, the instruction and interrupt cycles and stack organization in COA; closures, candidate keys and normalization in DBMS; infix to postfix, queues and tree traversals in DSA; JDK/JVM/JRE, wrapper classes and "find the output" in Java; Gauss-Seidel, Simpson's rules and Lin-Bairstow in CONMP. The last seven days are for making those answers automatic.

## The rule for the whole week

**Practise writing, not reading.** Reading notes feels productive but most of it is forgotten by the exam hall. Every session below ends with you writing answers from memory and then checking them against the solved papers.

Three sources are enough:
- the [past papers with solutions](/papers) (what is actually asked),
- each subject's **Exam guide** in the [Library](/library) (what to write, common mistakes),
- the [CONMP formula sheet](/library/conmp/formula-sheet) for numericals.

## Day 7: Map the paper

1. For each subject, open every past paper and list the questions that appear **two or more times**. This list is your syllabus for the week.
2. Mark each question green (can write it now), amber (know it, can't write it fully) or red (no idea).
3. Note the paper pattern: MCQs, 3-mark, 5-mark and 7-mark parts, and how many you may choose. In the mid-sem (60 marks, 2 hours) you choose 3 of 4, 4 of 5 and 3 of 4. Choice means you can safely drop one or two red topics per section; it does not mean you can skip a whole unit.

## Day 6 and Day 5: Red and amber topics, numericals first

- Spend the mornings on **numerical and program questions** (CONMP methods, Booth's algorithm, binary arithmetic, FD closures, SQL, Java programs, tree and graph traces). These are marks you either get fully or lose fully, and they only stick through practice.
- For each method: read one worked solution, close it, solve the same question on paper, then solve a second question from another paper.
- Afternoons: amber theory questions. Write each answer in the shape described in [how to write a 7-mark answer](/guides/7-mark-answer): definition, diagram, points, example.

## Day 4: First full paper under exam conditions

Take one complete past paper for your first exam, set a timer (2 hours for a mid-sem, 3 hours for an end-sem) and write it without notes. Then mark it honestly against the solutions. Every mistake goes into a **mistakes list** of one line each, for example "Simpson 3/8: weight 2 only on indices that are multiples of 3".

## Day 3: Fix the mistakes list

Redo every question on the mistakes list. Make a **one-page sheet per subject**: formulas, the steps of each algorithm, the three or four diagrams you must draw (bus system, instruction cycle flowchart, three-level DBMS architecture, JVM/JRE/JDK boxes, thread life cycle). Draw the diagrams from memory twice.

## Day 2: Second full paper

Write a different paper under the same conditions. Your score should rise; if a topic is still red, decide now whether to drop it (if the choice in that section allows) and spend the time on amber topics instead.

## Day 1: Light revision only

- Read the one-page sheets and the mistakes list. Re-draw the diagrams once.
- Do two or three short numericals to keep your hand in. No new topics.
- Pack your hall ticket, ID card, pens, pencil, scale and a non-programmable calculator if it is allowed (the paper instructions say whether it is; check with your faculty beforehand).
- **Sleep 7–8 hours.** Memory consolidates during sleep; an all-nighter costs more marks than it gains.

## When exams are back to back

The Semester 3 exams are often one or two days apart. Then compress the plan per subject: one day of red/amber topics and a full paper, and the evening before for the one-page sheet. Start the plan for the hardest subject earliest, before the exam week begins.

## In the exam hall

- Spend the first 5 minutes reading the whole paper and ticking the questions you will attempt.
- Answer your strongest questions first, but **write the question numbers exactly** as printed.
- Budget time by marks: in a 60-mark, 2-hour paper that is about 2 minutes per mark, so a 7-mark answer gets about 12 minutes. Move on when the time is up and come back if time remains.
- Leave the last 10 minutes to check numbering, units, signs in numericals and that every chosen question has an answer.

7-mark-answer.title: How to write a 7-mark answer
7-mark-answer.description: The structure that earns full marks on long questions: definition, labelled diagram, explanation in points, example and comparison, plus how to present code and numericals.
7-mark-answer.body:
A 7-mark question in a Semester 3 paper is marked against a scheme: definition, diagram, explanation, example, and sometimes a comparison or algorithm. Long answers that miss those parts lose marks, and short answers that hit every part often get full marks. This guide shows the structure that works for theory questions in COA, DBMS, DSA and Java, and a separate one for numericals.

## How much to write

In a 60-mark, 2-hour mid-sem you have about **2 minutes per mark**, so roughly **12 minutes for a 7-mark answer**, after leaving time to read and check. That is about **one to one and a half pages** of normal handwriting, including a diagram. In a 100-mark, 3-hour end-sem the budget is about 1.8 minutes per mark. If you are still writing after 15 minutes, finish the current point and move on.

## The structure for theory questions

**1. Definition (1 mark).** One or two precise sentences, using the textbook terms. *"Pipelining is a technique of decomposing a sequential process into sub-operations, each executed in a dedicated segment that operates concurrently with all other segments."*

**2. Diagram (1–2 marks).** Draw it whenever the topic has one: block diagrams, flowcharts, tables, trees, memory layouts. Use a pencil and a scale, label every box and arrow, and give it a caption. A clear diagram often earns marks even when the text is thin, and examiners look for it first.

**3. Explanation in points (2–3 marks).** Numbered or bulleted points, one idea each, with the key word in bold or underlined. Explain the working step by step, in the order it happens (for example fetch → decode → execute → interrupt check).

**4. Example (1 mark).** A small worked example, an RTL statement, a short code snippet or a real-world case. *"For 4 instructions in a 4-segment pipeline: 4 + 4 − 1 = 7 cycles instead of 16."*

**5. Advantages, disadvantages or comparison (1 mark), if relevant.** Two or three points each, or a small table when the question says "compare" or "differentiate".

**6. One-line conclusion (optional).** Ties the answer back to the question.

## "Differentiate" and "compare" questions

Always use a **table** with at least **five or six rows**, each row one basis of comparison (definition, speed, cost, flexibility, example…). Put the basis in the first column. A table is faster to write, easier to mark, and shows you know the parameters of comparison. Add one short example under the table if the question asks for it.

## Questions with code (Java, DSA)

- Write a **complete, compilable** program: imports, class, `main`, and the method asked for. Missing semicolons and braces cost marks.
- Use **meaningful names** and a short comment on each logical block.
- Show the **output** in a box after the program, for the sample input you choose.
- For algorithms, give the **algorithm or pseudocode first**, then a **trace** on a small input (a table of the stack, queue or array after each step), then the time complexity.

## Numerical questions (CONMP, COA arithmetic, DBMS closures)

- Write the **formula first**, with every symbol identified (*"Simpson's 1/3 rule, n = 6 even, h = 0.2"*). The formula alone often carries a mark.
- Show the **working in a table** (iterations, ordinates, differences, k-values), with the same number of decimal places in every row.
- **Box the final answer**, with units, and state the accuracy reached (*"correct to 3 decimal places since x₄ and x₅ agree"*).
- If the paper has a misprint or a missing value, **state your assumption** in one line and carry on; that is what the instructions ask for.

## Common ways to lose marks

- Writing a 5-mark answer for a 7-mark question (no diagram, no example).
- A diagram with no labels or no caption.
- Long paragraphs that hide the key words.
- Answering a different question that "looks similar". Re-read the question and answer exactly the parts asked: "explain with diagram **and** RTL statements" needs both.
- Not numbering the answer the same way as the paper (Q3(b), not "3.2").

## Practise it

Pick any 7-mark question from the [solved papers](/papers), set a 12-minute timer and write your answer. Then compare it with the CampusLoop solution, part by part: definition, diagram, points, example. Two or three of these per subject before the exam make the structure automatic. For the full revision schedule, see the [last 7 days plan](/guides/last-7-days).
